extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; aspiring novelists and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and composing novels, presenting core evaluative dimensions (story, people, plot, fantasy, prophecy, pattern, rhythm) and related craft criteria for critics and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story (fundamental aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental aspect of the novel is its story-telling aspect: a story is "a narrative of events arranged in their time sequence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a story it has one merit — making the audience want to know what happens next — and one fault — making the audience not want to know what happens next. The story is primitive and ancient, the backbone (or "tape-worm") of a novel; it cannot be abolished inside the fabric of a novel though it may be manipulated (hidden, inverted, altered hands on the clock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit/fault criterion for a story
rubrics_metrics.description: "Qua story, it can only have one merit: that of making the audience want to know what happens next. And conversely it can only have one fault: that of making the audience not want to know what happens next."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a basic litmus test for the storytelling element: does it sustain curiosity/suspense? If not, the story-as-story fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs Plot distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A story (sequence of events in time) is not the same as a plot; the plot is "an organism of a higher type."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate mere chronological narration with artistic plotting; evaluate whether events are merely 'and then' or organized into a higher, causally and artistically coherent structure (plot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice / oral quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is the repository of a voice and is the aspect that asks to be read aloud; it appeals to the ear as oratory does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the narrative voice functions when spoken — does it gain or lose effect? The voice can transform readers into listeners and contributes to the story's appeal even if it gives less of the author's personality than other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspense (the weapon of Scheherazade) is the primary literary tool for making the audience want to know 'what happens next.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and employ devices that create curiosity and delay resolution; suspense can be decisive even when other literary gifts are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-sense / life in time
rubrics_metrics.description: The story narrates the 'life in time' — events arranged chronologically — and the novel must maintain a time thread (there is always a clock) even when time is manipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a work handles chronology: honest chronological progression, concealed clocks (Brontë), inverted clocks (Sterne), or altered hands (Proust) are legitimate but the time-sense must remain intelligible to avoid blunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life by values (beyond time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily life comprises both life in time and life by "values" (moments measured by intensity rather than minutes); a good novel includes the life by values as well as the life in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate devices that convey intensity, memory, anticipation, and value-based experience; a novel's greatness often depends on integrating both senses of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of space vs sense of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Some novels emphasize time (e.g., Arnold Bennett's The Old Wives' Tale), others make space the dominant force (e.g., Tolstoy's War and Peace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the work's grandeur or musical effect arises from its handling of spatial breadth (landscape, national canvas) as well as temporal breadth, and how space and time interact to produce aesthetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel's sensitiveness (medium sensitivity over subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's success "lies in its own sensitiveness, not in the success of its subject matter" — the medium developing because it acquires new sensitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how sensitively the author handles the medium (tone, perception, nuance), rather than relying on topical or historical importance of subject matter to confer value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial personality and human quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The intensely human quality of the novel is unavoidable; the final test of a novel will be our affection for it; the author's personality is best conveyed through characters, plot, or comments on life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess emotional resonance, humanity, and whether the novel invites genuine affection rather than sentimentality; consider whether characters and plot communicate the author's personality effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality (beware its dominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimentality will lurk in criticism and can distort judgment: "I can promise that sentimentality shall not speak too loudly or too soon."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of allowing personal liking or easy sentiment to dominate critical assessment; aim to keep sentimentality from obscuring other evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition and technique vary historically
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary tradition (technique) is the borderland between literature and history and does alter from generation to generation (e.g., technique of laughing at characters, technique of fantasy, use of 'he said'/'she said').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, attend to tradition and historical technique: how execution differs across eras and how specific techniques place a work within a tradition or phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique of fantasy and execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy has techniques that differ among writers (e.g., Virginia Woolf's aim/effect may resemble Sterne's but execution differs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fantasy by its mode of execution as much as by its aim; similar aims can produce distinct effects depending on technique and phase of tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story-teller vs plot-weaver modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The story-teller profits by ragged ends and episodic 'and then' narration, while the plot-weaver constructs cause-and-effect and tight construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a novelist is operating as a story-teller (emphasizing suspense and episodic interest) or as a plot-weaver (seeking structural coherence), and judge success against the chosen mode's requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ragged ends and incidental episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: A story-teller can include incidents and 'ragged ends' that appear to lead nowhere but maintain reader curiosity; such loose threads are a legitimate device of storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penalize incidental or seemingly irrelevant episodes purely for lack of causal explanation if they serve the storyteller's aim of maintaining curiosity and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating novel development with historical progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronology and social/historical progress (e.g., women's movement, constitution) do not automatically develop the novel; the novel's medium changes through new sensitiveness, not merely by external historical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid simplistic historicist claims that social change directly equals artistic improvement; instead analyze changes in technique and sensibility within the medium itself.
